Use calculus to find the coordinates of the closest point to $P(5,-3)$ that is equidistant to the points $A(-2,1)$ and $B(6,1).$

The coordinates of the required point are
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}
$).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068082/assets/a86fbc456930e18159b1745f5a71fe82bf7075f3aa6d9fd4307a71a583a37a7a.png)

Note the following:

- The dotted line is the *perpendicular bisector* of the segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$

- All the points on this perpendicular bisector are equidistant to $A$ and $B.$

- Our task is to find the point $Q$ on this line that's closest to $P.$

First, we create a function $S$ which represents the *squared* distance between the point $P(5,-3)$ and a general point $Q(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-5)^{2}+(y-(-3))^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(y+3)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-10x+6y+34\end{aligned}
$$

The required point $Q(x,y)$ is equidistant to the points $A(-2,1)$ and $B(6,1).$ So, by writing down $(QA)^{2}=(QB)^{2},$ we have the following constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{(x+2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{(QA)^{2}} & ={{(x-6)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{(QB)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

We make $x$ the subject in the constraint equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =(x-6)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+4x+4+(y-1)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-12x+36+(y-1)^{2} \\ \cancel{{x}^{2}}+\cancel{(y-1)^{2}}+4x+4 & =\cancel{{x}^{2}}-12x+36+\cancel{(y-1)^{2}} \\ 4x+12x & =36-4 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our expression for $S(x,y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =(2)^{2}+{y}^{2}-10(2)+6y+34 \\  & =4+{y}^{2}-20+6y+34 \\  & ={y}^{2}+6y+18.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the first derivative,

$$
{S}^{′}(y)=2y+6,
$$

and solve ${S}^{′}(y)=0$ to find the stationary point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ 2y+6 & =0 \\ y & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Let's verify that this stationary point is a minimum. Taking the second derivative, we find

$$
{S}^{″}(-3)=2>0.
$$

We conclude that the stationary point $y=-3$ indeed minimizes the squared distance. 

Therefore, the required point is $(\,2,-3\,).$
